The uninvited guest - HIV

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
“The Uninvited guest” will be a novel way of talking about one of the most dire and uncomfortable topics - living with HIV in an inspirational way. It will combine the cutting edge science in the fight against HIV, the race to find a cure or a vaccine with the life lessons of those who have survived and experienced the journey over the last 21 years. But it’s a tired topic and so a dinner party filled with facts and humour will make it digestible

Summary:
Pholokgolo Ramothwala has been living with HIV for the last 21 years and having spent so many years obsessed with the topic, now he’s returned to his original life plan of being a Chef. He’s been a TAC activist and worked for Soul City and released a book last year “My life beyond HIV- what HIV has taught me in the last 21 years” Today he hosts diner parties and is invited as the Chef on celebrity weekend getaways, exploring gastronomical delights. It an intimate conversation with Devi- who also loves cooking, Pholo will host a sophisticated dinner party with Professional nurse Angela Motususi, Prof Francois Venter, and Dr Kathy Mngadi who co-hosts the HVTN 705 vaccine trial.

Further information:
The insert will start with Devi in the kitchen with Pholo learning some new cooking tips and discussing his more intimate journey. Then when the guests arrive over pre- drinks Devi and Pholo will introduce them. Over dinner discussion topics of Pholo desire for a cure , a vaccine, new treatment regimes will created the structure to explore the science. Francois Venter who is an old friend with Pholo will generate an easy rapport and could be a mixture of intense and light hearted.
The dinner discussion will cover the personal milestones and current cutting edge science- the desire for a cure vs vaccine and the change in medication. The Professors will also share their personal journey, what’s changed and what hasn’t.
When Pholo was infected 1000 people a day were being infected, that statistic remains the same today. Stigma remains an issue. Then there was no cure, so the feared getting ill haunted his youth. In the denialism years when Manto said garlic beetroot and sweet potatoes where a cure will generate some jokes from Devi. The TAC years were scary, he saw people dying in front of him and he had a small child. When they found cure the message shifted from prevention to getting people on the ARV’s. He sees that as a problem as to why the infection rates remain.
Pholo talks about the excitement earlier this year when the London patient was cured. This gives us an opportunity to look at that, the break through what happened and why it’s not an accessible option but why its cutting edge science for the potential of genetic modification using the interview with Dr Gupta. We will talk about ARV’s and the new regimes and impact on Pholo and the Angela. Stigma remains a problem, Pholo still has professional people calling him and asking “how did I get it” and stigma remains a barrier to treatment.

Script: For 41 year old Joburger Pholokgolo Ramothwala, having a good time means cooking, feeding people and good conversation across the dinner table.
UP NAT SOUND & CONVERSATION IN KITCHEN
Script: Pholo was a 21 year old student when he was diagnosed with HIV. It’s been a long journey grappling with the fear and stigma of it but he learnt not only to LIVE, but to THRIVE reinventing himself several times over– first as an Aids activist, then life coach and now chef.
UP NAT SOUND & CONVERSATION IN KITCHEN
Script: As I’m known to be the Curry Queen I’m joining Pholo to prepare a special curry for some of the hottest brains in healthcare, to discuss what science has in store for the 8 million South Africans, who like Pholo are living with HIV…
Devi 17 33 27: I think what's great, to be in a fantastic environment, eating your good food and talking HIV. I think 20 years ago we would never have done it like this.
Pholo [17:33:37] That's the whole point. Where people are living with HIV they should be living life beyond HIV. I see HIV as a secondary factor in my life.
Devi [16:34:23] So Pholo what's the plan?
Pholo [16:34:26] We're going gonna do a starter with a prawns [16:34:47] then I want to make lamb curry and I'm going to make chicken curry. And then with Basmati. Then I'll do like a pan-fried spinach .
Devi [16:35:03] Yum, yum, yum. Let's go.
Script: Outside of the kitchen, Pholo mentors young professionals. Even if amazing progress in HIV drugs has made it just another chronic illness, stigma remains real.
Pholo [16:49:43 So I work most with professionals lawyers and the people who don't want to go to Bara hospital for service.
Devi [16:50:04] do you find that the more professional you are, the less open you likely to be about your status? Yes
Pholo [17:03:16] I had someone who said to me I'm too educated how did I get infected?..[17:03:51] I find that most of these guys, they don't disclose their status, only their doctor. Then you'll be only the third person who knows about my status. That's the common line
Pholo [17:36:30] I think I've done it I am happily Yep. Yes. The chicken is there. I'm just going to let it simmer a little bit more.
Script: Pholo’s invited his oldest friend, Professor Francois Venter, once an activist doctor fighting for basic treatment…now leading investigations into ground-breaking studies for a cure.
UPS FRANCOIS
And he's always wanted to meet Dr Katherine Mngadi to get the low-down on how far vaccines are in preventing HIV
UPS KATHERINE
Angela Motsusi, a nurse, HIV positive is a motivational speaker.
UPS ANGELA
and Dr Moeketsi Mathe, works in private practice
Devi” So I have been helping out in the kitchen and I am starving let’s eat
Devi [19:12:58] So I have to say, as I dig into my beetroot, I mean, the most obvious question for me right now is what was it like for you guys as doctors, as activists during that time when we were in complete denial of the country?
Angela [19:15:33] There were long waiting lists before you could get onto ART there were a lot of hurdles and as a result people died
Pholo [19:17:18] you know, when you're living with HIV and you keep going bury people. Pholo [19:17:58] Yeah, yeah, yeah. You know, at some point its going to be me And it was quite hectic.
Moekestsi [19:20:05] there actually wasn't an incentive to test because what's the point of testing if you find out you are positive, the health system got nothing to offer you.
Script: Since then the scientific breakthroughs have been incredible. Earlier this year hopes were raised when the second HIV-positive man, known as the London patient was cured. It came a decade after the so-called Berlin patient had similar results
Devi [20:11:49] So no wonder people are going to get excited and think, well, it should be just around the corner. But is it?
Francois [20:08:58] I think it's a very complicated problem. [20:16:10] So these patients had cancers, leukemias, lymphomas, and they did what we call a stem cell transplant, which fundamentally changed the genetic makeup, which meant the way they dealt with the virus was different.
It was a way of killing the leukemia lymphoma and it was a way of killing the virus at the same time as a happy bystander. It wasn't the primary reason to actually giving the stem cell transplant.[20:16:33] STEM cell transplants are very, very toxic and while we have got better at them it still way outstrips the toxicity of antiretroviral therapy.
Devi [20:12:47] When you heard about the cure. I mean, what was your initial reaction?
Pholo [20:13:16] I kind of didn't get excited. And I remember posting on my social media that do not get excited. ….and its psychologically, you know, people take their meds they are caring on, they're fine.[20:13:57] But when is the cure coming You know, it's been something that I would love to know.
Angela [20:14:07] you know, the life expectancy of an HIV positive person is much longer than what it used to be. So if it comes, yay I'm going to be happy. But for now, I'm quite happy with the treatments. Yeah.
Script: Then there hope of a vaccine which katherine has she spent the last 16 years working on. There are 3 trials running in South Africa at the moment and she’s co-chairs the trial on HIV-negative Southern-African women, which seems to be showing hope for protection against a variety of global HIV strains.
Devi [20:19:45] So how far away could we be then from a vaccine?
Katherine [20:45:57] Well, 2022, we'll have our first answers about three current studies that are in the field and one of those studies [20:21:36] We're actually planning for the partial efficacy. ... you can prevent anywhere between 5 to 15 million infections in a 15 year period so myself I am super excited [20:22:12] …. because the early studies in humans have shown that it's actually it does teach the immune system.20:23:03] ...So for myself, I feel extremely hopeful... that's what drives me on a daily basis.
Script: This is the strongest result to date and the closest we have ever been out of the 80 trials run in the past 20 years
Pholo [20:46:29] So I will call you in 2020
[20:46:34] Call me.
Francois [20:23:59] From a jeek perspective at some of the most amazing sciene its teaching us so much stuff about the vaccine field in general, not just HIV
Devi [20:24:11] And it's happening here.
Francois [20:24:12] Yes, it's incredible, some of the best scientists in the world are housed in SA.
Script: Spirits at the table are up, there’s been a 44% reduction in new infections in just 5 years, the test and treat programme appears to be working,
It’s been a good year for Francois, apart from the release of a new treatment, TDL which lowers the viral load quickly, is safer and cheaper, his collaborative research into killing the virus, while it lies dormant in inaccessible reservoirs in the body, is what really excites him
Francois [20:24:28] So the virus is very smart and hides out in deep, dark parts of your body, even though we can clear out the blood from the of replicating virus. It lives in your brain and your guts and your spleen your bone. And actually it just sits dormant. [20:24:56] We were talking about as shocking them into unveiling themselves and declaring that that particular cell is HIV positive so your immune system can come and clear it. It's been a huge challenge. We got drugs that probably can unlock ninety nine point nine percent of the viruses, but you just need that point, one percent still to be positive and they'll still come back
Moeketsi [20:12:05] We're still being outsmarted by this virus. That's the problem [20:12:32]. You can come up with a new weapon and it builds a new defense system
Script: Just extracting the samples has been a massive achievement, and despite not having the silver bullet yet, it holds great promise for letting us know if a cure is feasible'
Devi [20:47:33] So let’s throw forward. How do you see your futures?
Angela. What I would like to see happening is getting to a place where we have actually normalized HIV, we can treat it as like any other normal chronic illness where we can have normal conversations around it
Pholo [20:50:20] The best thing is to live your life beyond HIV and do other things with your life. There is 8 million of us, you know, you can’t ignore that
Script: As the dinner wound down I was struck by how excited and committed they remain to one of the biggest health burdens and science mysteries of our time.
